zero-off-diagonal-metric-tensor-componen.intuitive_summary: Imagine a perfect grid on a map where all lines intersect at 90-degree angles. Moving a tiny step east and a tiny step north creates a right-angled triangle. The total distance squared is simply the sum of the squares of the east and north movements. The condition $g_{ij}=0$ for $i \neq j$ means the coordinate system behaves like this perfect grid locally; the axes don't 'mix' or 'shear' when measuring small distances.

numerical-value-of-gravitational-constan.title: Approximate Numerical Value of the Gravitational Constant (G)
numerical-value-of-gravitational-constan.description: This represents the approximate numerical value of the Newtonian gravitational constant, $G$, a fundamental physical constant quantifying the strength of the gravitational force between massive objects.
numerical-value-of-gravitational-constan.conceptual_definition: The numerical value $6.674 \times 10^{-11}$ is the experimentally determined proportionality constant, denoted as $G$, in Newton's law of universal gravitation, $F = G \frac{m_1 m_2}{r^2}$. It represents the magnitude of the gravitational force in Newtons between two one-kilogram masses separated by a distance of one meter.
numerical-value-of-gravitational-constan.interpretation: This specific numerical value, $6.674 \times 10^{-11}$, represents the approximate, experimentally determined magnitude of the gravitational constant $G$ in the International System of Units (SI). It quantifies the strength of the gravitational interaction, meaning it dictates the amount of gravitational force exerted between two masses at a given distance. For instance, two 1 kg masses separated by 1 meter would attract each other with a force of approximately $6.674 \times 10^{-11}$ Newtons. The precise measurement of $G$ is notoriously difficult but critical for accurate calculations in celestial mechanics, astrophysics, and cosmology, influencing our understanding of planetary orbits, stellar evolution, and the large-scale structure of the universe.
numerical-value-of-gravitational-constan.limits_and_boundary: The gravitational constant $G$ is considered a fundamental constant of nature and is assumed to be invariant across all spacetime coordinates and physical conditions. Its value does not depend on temperature $T$, velocity $v$, or spatial separation $r$. In the classical limit where Planck's constant $\hbar \to 0$, gravity as described by $G$ remains the dominant long-range force for massive objects.
numerical-value-of-gravitational-constan.symmetry_origin: The constant $G$ is a fundamental coupling constant within the framework of General Relativity, a theory founded on the principle of general covariance (diffeomorphism invariance). It sets the scale for how spacetime geometry responds to the presence of mass-energy.

G.name: Newtonian Gravitational Constant
G.description: The empirical physical constant quantifying the magnitude of the gravitational force between two bodies.

numerical-value-of-gravitational-constan.intuitive_summary: The gravitational constant $G$ is an incredibly small number, which explains why gravity is the weakest of the four fundamental forces and is only noticeable for objects with very large mass, like planets and stars.

dimensionless-hubble-parameter-definitio.title: Dimensionless Hubble Parameter Definition
dimensionless-hubble-parameter-definitio.description: This equation defines the dimensionless Hubble parameter, 'h', by normalizing the Hubble constant ($H_0$) to a reference value of 100 km s\textsuperscript{-1} Mpc\textsuperscript{-1}.
dimensionless-hubble-parameter-definitio.conceptual_definition: The Hubble constant ( $H_0$) quantifies the current rate at which the universe is expanding. Due to historical uncertainties and varying measurement units, it is common in cosmology to define a dimensionless parameter, $h$, by dividing $H_0$ by a standard reference value of 100 km s$\textsuperscript{-1}$ Mpc$\textsuperscript{-1}$. This normalization simplifies the expression and comparison of other cosmological parameters, making calculations more consistent across different studies.
dimensionless-hubble-parameter-definitio.interpretation: The dimensionless Hubble parameter, $h$, is a critical scaling factor in the standard model of cosmology. It allows for the expression of various cosmological densities, such as the physical density of cold dark matter ($\Omega_c h^2$) or baryonic matter ($\Omega_b h^2$), in a way that is independent of the precise, and often debated, value of $H_0$. This convention facilitates easier comparison of observational results and theoretical predictions, as many cosmological quantities are proportional to powers of $h$. For example, the age of the universe and the distance to cosmological objects depend inversely on $h$.
dimensionless-hubble-parameter-definitio.limits_and_boundary: The value of $h$ must be positive, reflecting the observed expansion of the universe. Current cosmological observations constrain $h$ to be approximately between 0.67 and 0.74, although there is a persistent tension between local and cosmic microwave background measurements. There are no theoretical upper or lower bounds other than being positive, but observational constraints are tight.
dimensionless-hubble-parameter-definitio.symmetry_origin: This formula is a definitional convention rather than a direct consequence of fundamental symmetries or conservation laws. However, the Hubble constant ( $H_0$) itself is a parameter within the Friedmann equations, which are derived from Einstein's field equations under the assumption of the cosmological principle (homogeneity and isotropy of the universe), embodying symmetries of spacetime on large scales.

H_0.name: H_0
H_0.description: The Hubble constant, representing the current expansion rate of the universe. Its units are typically expressed as km s\textsuperscript{-1} Mpc\textsuperscript{-1} (kilometers per second per megaparsec).

h.name: h
h.description: The dimensionless Hubble parameter, defined as the Hubble constant divided by 100 km s\textsuperscript{-1} Mpc\textsuperscript{-1}. It is a unitless scaling factor used in cosmological calculations.

hadamard-basis-plus-state-eea52028.title: Hadamard Basis State |+⟩
hadamard-basis-plus-state-eea52028.description: A fundamental single-qubit state representing an equal superposition of the computational basis states $|0\rangle$ and $|1\rangle$. It is a key resource in quantum computing and information theory.
hadamard-basis-plus-state-eea52028.conceptual_definition: The Hadamard basis state, denoted as $|+\rangle$, is defined as the normalized linear combination of the computational basis states $|0\rangle$ and $|1\rangle$ with equal positive amplitudes: $|+\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} (|0\rangle + |1\rangle)$. It is one of the two eigenstates of the Pauli-X operator.
hadamard-basis-plus-state-eea52028.interpretation: A qubit prepared in the $|+\rangle$ state, when measured in the computational basis $\{|0\rangle, |1\rangle\}$, has a probability of $|\langle 0 | + \rangle|^2 = 1/2$ of collapsing to the state $|0\rangle$ and a probability of $|\langle 1 | + \rangle|^2 = 1/2$ of collapsing to the state $|1\rangle$. The $|+\rangle$ state is an eigenstate of the Pauli-X operator ($\hat{\sigma}_x$) with an eigenvalue of $+1$, as shown by $\hat{\sigma}_x |+\rangle = |+\rangle$. This invariance under a bit-flip operation is crucial. Geometrically, on the Bloch sphere, the $|+\rangle$ state vector points along the positive x-axis. This state is fundamental for creating quantum parallelism in algorithms like the Deutsch-Jozsa and Shor's algorithms.
hadamard-basis-plus-state-eea52028.limits_and_boundary: In the presence of strong environmental decoherence, the superposition characteristic of the $|+\rangle$ state is destroyed. The off-diagonal terms of its density matrix, $\rho = |+\rangle\langle+|$, decay to zero. This process transforms the pure state into a classical mixed state $\rho \to \frac{1}{2}(|0\rangle\langle0| + |1\rangle\langle1|)$, which represents a classical bit with a 50% probability of being 0 or 1, having lost all quantum phase information.
hadamard-basis-plus-state-eea52028.symmetry_origin: The invariance of the $|+\rangle$ state under the Pauli-X bit-flip operation ($\hat{\sigma}_x |+\rangle = |+\rangle$) reflects a discrete symmetry. This eigenstate property is a manifestation of the underlying SU(2) group structure of single-qubit transformations, where the Pauli-X operator is one of the generators.

|+\\rangle.name: Hadamard Plus State
|+\\rangle.description: A single-qubit state vector representing an equal superposition of the computational basis states.

|0\\rangle.name: Computational Basis State Zero

hadamard-basis-plus-state-eea52028.intuitive_summary: Imagine a quantum coin spinning perfectly, having an exactly equal chance of landing heads ($|0\rangle$) or tails ($|1\rangle$) upon measurement. The $|+\rangle$ state is the mathematical description of this 'spinning' state before the outcome is known.

expectation-value-of-product-of-observab.title: Expectation Value of a Product of Observables
expectation-value-of-product-of-observab.description: This quantity represents the quantum mechanical expectation value for the joint measurement of two observables, $A_i$ and $B_j$. It is a fundamental component in calculating correlation functions, particularly in the context of Bell's theorem and entangled systems.
expectation-value-of-product-of-observab.conceptual_definition: The expectation value $\langle A_i B_j \rangle$ quantifies the statistical correlation between the outcomes of measuring two observables, represented by Hermitian operators $\hat{A}_i$ and $\hat{B}_j$. This value is calculated by averaging the product of the eigenvalues of $\hat{A}_i$ and $\hat{B}_j$, weighted by the probabilities of their joint occurrence as determined by the system's quantum state. For a composite system in a state described by the density matrix $\hat{\rho}$, this is formally given by $\text{Tr}(\hat{\rho} (\hat{A}_i \otimes \hat{B}_j))$.
expectation-value-of-product-of-observab.interpretation: This term, $\langle A_i B_j \rangle$, specifically measures the correlation between two distinct quantum measurements, represented by observables $\hat{A}_i$ and $\hat{B}_j$. These are often performed on different, spatially separated parts of an entangled system. A value of $\langle A_i B_j \rangle$ close to $+1$ indicates strong positive correlation (e.g., if measuring $\hat{A}_i$ yields $+1$, measuring $\hat{B}_j$ is also highly likely to yield $+1$). Conversely, a value close to $-1$ indicates strong anti-correlation (if $\hat{A}_i$ yields $+1$, $\hat{B}_j$ is likely to yield $-1$). A value near $0$ suggests no significant statistical correlation between the measurement outcomes. In the context of Bell inequalities, these expectation values are the fundamental building blocks used to construct the Bell parameter $S$, which tests the predictions of quantum mechanics against those of local realism.
expectation-value-of-product-of-observab.limits_and_boundary: For a system in a product state $|\Psi\rangle = |\psi_A\rangle \otimes |\psi_B\rangle$ (i.e., not entangled), the expectation value factorizes: $\langle A_i B_j \rangle = \langle A_i \rangle \langle B_j \rangle$. In the classical limit where $\hbar \to 0$, this corresponds to a classical statistical average over a phase space distribution. For maximally entangled states, the correlation can be maximal, e.g., $|\langle A_i B_j \rangle| = 1$, which violates Bell inequalities and demonstrates non-locality.
expectation-value-of-product-of-observab.symmetry_origin: Not applicable; this is a statistical definition derived from the measurement postulate of quantum mechanics. However, the value itself can be constrained by symmetries of the state or Hamiltonian.

A_i.name: Observable A
A_i.description: A quantum observable, represented by a Hermitian operator $\hat{A}_i$. The index $i$ often denotes a specific measurement setting or basis choice.

B_j.name: Observable B
B_j.description: A quantum observable, represented by a Hermitian operator $\hat{B}_j$. The index $j$ often denotes a specific measurement setting or basis choice for a second party or subsystem.

\\langle \\cdot \\rangle.name: Expectation Value
\\langle \\cdot \\rangle.description: The quantum mechanical expectation value, which gives the statistical average of an observable's measurement outcomes over a large number of identical preparations of a quantum state.

expectation-value-of-product-of-observab.intuitive_summary: Imagine measuring two different properties on a pair of connected quantum particles. This value tells you, on average, how the outcome of the first measurement relates to the outcome of the second. A positive value means they tend to agree, a negative value means they tend to disagree, and zero means they are independent.

wavefunction-of-a-quantum-state-eda904c3.title: Position-Space Wavefunction for a Quantum State
wavefunction-of-a-quantum-state-eda904c3.description: A complex-valued function, $\psi_m(x)$, that describes the quantum state of a particle in one dimension. Its squared modulus, $|\psi_m(x)|^2$, represents the probability density of finding the particle at position $x$.
wavefunction-of-a-quantum-state-eda904c3.conceptual_definition: The wavefunction, $\psi_m(x)$, is a solution to the time-independent Schrödinger equation for a specific quantum state labeled by the index $m$. It is a mathematical object that contains all knowable information about a quantum system in that state, within the position representation. The set of all such functions for a given system, $\{\psi_m(x)\}$, forms a basis for the Hilbert space of possible states.
wavefunction-of-a-quantum-state-eda904c3.interpretation: The physical interpretation of the wavefunction $\psi_m(x)$ is probabilistic, as dictated by the Born rule. The quantity $|\psi_m(x)|^2 dx$ gives the probability of finding the particle in the infinitesimal interval between $x$ and $x+dx$. The function $\psi_m(x)$ itself is a complex number, often written as $R(x)e^{iS(x)/\hbar}$, where its magnitude $R(x)$ relates to probability density and the spatial gradient of its phase, $\nabla S(x)$, is proportional to the particle's momentum. For a bound system, the index $m$ typically represents a discrete quantum number (e.g., an energy level), and the set of wavefunctions $\{\psi_m(x)\}$ forms a complete orthonormal basis.
wavefunction-of-a-quantum-state-eda904c3.limits_and_boundary: For a bound state, the wavefunction must be square-integrable, which implies it must vanish at infinity: $\lim_{|x| \to \infty} \psi_m(x) = 0$. In the classical limit, as $\hbar \to 0$, the rapid oscillations of the wavefunction's phase lead to destructive interference everywhere except along the classical trajectory, recovering classical mechanics through the WKB approximation or Ehrenfest's theorem.
wavefunction-of-a-quantum-state-eda904c3.symmetry_origin: The conservation of probability, a core property of the wavefunction, is a direct consequence of the global U(1) gauge symmetry of the Schrödinger equation. This means the physics is invariant under a global phase shift of the wavefunction, $\psi \to e^{i\alpha}\psi$.

\\psi_m.name: Wavefunction for state m
\\psi_m.description: The position-space wavefunction for the quantum state labeled by the index $m$.

m.name: Quantum State Index
m.description: An index, often a quantum number (like an energy level), that labels a specific eigenstate of the system.

x.name: Position Coordinate

momentum-operator-in-position-basis-61b3.title: Momentum Operator (x-component) in Position Representation
momentum-operator-in-position-basis-61b3.description: This rule defines the representation of the x-component of the linear momentum operator, often written as $\hat{p}_x$, in the position basis of quantum mechanics. It shows that momentum acts as a differential operator on the spatial coordinates of a wavefunction.
momentum-operator-in-position-basis-61b3.conceptual_definition: In the position representation of quantum mechanics, where a particle's state is described by a wavefunction $\Psi(x)$, the physical observable of momentum along the x-axis is represented by the Hermitian operator $\hat{p}_x$. This operator is defined as the partial derivative with respect to position $x$, scaled by the factor $-i\hbar$.
momentum-operator-in-position-basis-61b3.interpretation: The expression $\hat{p}_x = -i\hbar \frac{\partial}{\partial x}$ is a foundational postulate of quantum mechanics. It establishes that the momentum operator $\hat{p}_x$ acts on a position-space wavefunction $\Psi(x)$ to yield information about the particle's momentum. The presence of the imaginary unit $i$ is essential to ensure the operator is Hermitian ($\hat{p}_x = \hat{p}_x^\dagger$), which guarantees that its eigenvalues (the possible measurement outcomes for momentum) are real numbers. The reduced Planck constant $\hbar$ sets the fundamental scale for this quantum relationship, linking momentum to the spatial variation of the wavefunction.
momentum-operator-in-position-basis-61b3.limits_and_boundary: In the classical limit, as the reduced Planck constant $\hbar \to 0$, the commutator between the position and momentum operators, $[\hat{x}, \hat{p}_x] = i\hbar$, vanishes. This restores the classical picture where position $x$ and momentum $p_x$ are commuting variables that can be simultaneously determined with arbitrary precision. In this limit, $p_x$ ceases to be a differential operator and becomes a simple scalar quantity.
momentum-operator-in-position-basis-61b3.symmetry_origin: The momentum operator $\hat{p}_x$ is the quantum mechanical generator of infinitesimal spatial translations along the x-axis. This relationship is a direct consequence of the deep connection between symmetry and conservation laws, articulated by Noether's theorem. The invariance of physical laws under spatial translation implies the conservation of linear momentum.
